entries.title: Mise en place
entries.summary: Mise en place, everything in its place, is the work a cook does before the first ticket: ingredients prepared, tools set out and a plan in the head, so that service is spent cooking rather than searching.
entries.guest: Mise en place means everything in its place: a kitchen prepares every ingredient before the doors open, so each plate can be cooked the moment it is ordered.

paras: Mise en place (meez ahn PLAHS) is French for putting in place, and kitchens use it to mean everything in its place: every ingredient prepared, every tool at hand and a plan for the service ahead, all set before the first ticket arrives. A cook with good mise spends service cooking. A cook without it spends service hunting for a spoon while the hollandaise splits and the fish overcooks.

It matters because a rush leaves no time to think twice. Every minute spent peeling a shallot during service is a minute a plate waits under the lamp. Mise en place moves the slow, careful work into the quiet hours, so the busy hours run on speed and repetition.

Building a station starts with the board. Lay a damp cloth or a non-slip mat under it so it cannot slide, because a board that moves is how cooks cut themselves. Set the knives beside it, with two or three dry side towels folded at hand: a dry towel for lifting hot pans, never a wet one, which carries heat straight into the hand. Ninth pans, small steel inserts a ninth the size of a full hotel pan, hold the cut vegetables in a row within arm's reach, with salt, pepper and oils where the hand finds them without looking. Add a bowl for scraps and a sanitiser bucket with its cloth.

The prep list says what to make today; the par says how much. A par is the quantity of each item a station needs on hand for one service, set by the chef from the covers, the number of guests expected. Before setting up, a sauce cook reads the book, the reservation list, to see how many covers are booked, when the rush lands and whether a large party may order the same dish at once. The cook then counts what is left from yesterday, takes it from the par and makes the difference.

At a sauce station the mise is exact. Clarified butter sits warm, never hot, ready for hollandaise. The vinegar, shallot and tarragon reduction for béarnaise is made and strained. Shallots are ciselé, cut into fine, even dice with a sharp knife so they are cut, not crushed. Herbs are picked, the leaves pulled from their stems. Stocks are hot at the back of the stove, so a pan sauce can be built in the minutes a steak rests.

Working clean as you go is part of the mise, not a chore after it. Wipe the board between jobs, sweep scraps into the scrap bowl rather than pushing them to the edge, and change a towel once it is wet. Every container that goes into the fridge carries a label: what it is, the date it was made, the cook's initials and the use-by date the kitchen sets. Under the FDA Food Code, most perishable ready-to-eat foods made in the kitchen and kept at 5°C (41°F) or colder must be used or thrown away within seven days, the day they were made counting as day one.

In the end mise en place is a habit of mind. The cook who has it thinks one step ahead of the ticket: while one plate cooks, the next pan is heating and the garnish for the third is in reach. Chefs read a cook's head from the state of the station.

Servers keep a mise of their own: pens, a crumber, a wine key, polished glasses and the notes from lineup, the short meeting before service where the day's food is explained. At Brennan's, which Gulf fish is running today is learned at lineup, and so are the varieties in Maggie's Mushrooms and how they are cooked. A server who reaches the table already knowing has good mise.

faults.fault: Running out of a sauce or garnish in the middle of service
faults.cause: The par was set without reading the book, or yesterday's leftovers were not counted.
faults.fix: Read the reservations before prepping, prep to par with a margin for a large party, and tell the chef early if stock runs low.

faults.cause: The prep list was not finished, or the slow jobs were left until last.
faults.fix: Do the slow jobs first, such as stocks, reductions and clarified butter, and finish the whole list before the first ticket.

faults.cause: No damp cloth or mat beneath it.
faults.fix: Set a damp cloth or non-slip mat under every board before the first cut.

faults.cause: It was filled in a hurry and put away.
faults.fix: Label and date every container as it is filled; anything unknown goes to the chef, who usually has it thrown away.

cards.front: What does mise en place mean in a kitchen?
cards.back: Everything in its place: ingredients prepared, tools set out and a plan made before the first ticket, so service is spent cooking, not searching.

cards.front: Why does a cutting board sit on a damp cloth or mat?
cards.back: So it cannot slide. A board that moves under the knife is one of the commonest ways cooks cut themselves.

cards.front: Why does a cook lift hot pans with a dry side towel, never a wet one?
cards.back: Water carries heat far faster than dry cloth, so a wet towel sends the pan's heat straight into the hand.

cards.front: What are ninth pans, and what goes in them?
cards.back: Small steel inserts, a ninth the size of a full hotel pan, holding cut vegetables, herbs and garnishes in a row within arm's reach.

cards.front: What is a par on a prep list?
cards.back: The quantity of each item a station needs on hand for one service, set by the chef from the covers expected.

cards.front: Why does a sauce cook read the book before setting up?
cards.back: The reservation book shows how many covers are coming, when the rush lands and whether a large party may order at once, which sets how much to make.

cards.front: Name four items of a sauce station's mise en place.
cards.back: Warm clarified butter, a strained béarnaise reduction, shallots ciselé and picked herbs, with stocks hot at the back of the stove.

cards.front: Why are the shallots ciselé before service, not as each ticket comes in?
cards.back: Cutting them fine and even takes time a rush does not have; done ahead, they wait in a ninth pan for the béarnaise and the pan sauces.

cards.front: What goes on the label of every container in the fridge?
cards.back: What it is, the date it was made, the cook's initials and the use-by date the kitchen sets.

cards.front: How long may most chilled, ready-to-eat prepared food be kept under the FDA Food Code?
cards.back: At most seven days at 5°C (41°F) or colder, with the day it was made counted as day one.

cards.front: What does it mean to cook one step ahead of the ticket?
cards.back: While one plate cooks, the next pan is heating and the next garnish is in reach, so nothing waits on the cook.

cards.front: What is a server's mise en place?
cards.back: Pens, a crumber, a wine key, polished glasses and the lineup notes, such as which Gulf fish is running today.

questions.q: What does a kitchen mean by mise en place?
questions.answer: Everything prepared and in place before service
distractors: The order in which plates leave the pass
The final garnish placed on a plate
The cleaning done after the last cover
questions.why: Mise en place is the preparation done before the first ticket: ingredients cut, tools set and a plan made, so service is spent cooking.

questions.q: Why does a cook set a damp cloth or mat under the cutting board?
distractors: To keep the knife edge sharp
To cool the board between jobs
questions.why: A board that moves under the knife is one of the commonest causes of cuts; the damp cloth grips the bench and holds it still.

questions.q: A cook reaches for a hot pan handle. Which towel should it be?
distractors: A towel soaked in cold water
questions.why: Water conducts heat far faster than dry cloth, so any wet towel sends the heat of the handle straight into the hand.

questions.q: In a professional kitchen, what is a station's par?
questions.answer: How much it needs on hand for one service
distractors: The time a dish takes to cook on the line
The price a dish must sell at to cover cost
Food part-cooked ahead to finish to order
questions.why: The chef sets a par for each item from the covers expected; the cook counts what is left and makes the difference.

questions.q: Why does a sauce cook read the reservation book before setting up?
questions.answer: To see the covers and when the rush lands
distractors: To learn the guests' names for the pass
To choose the wines the sauces should match
To decide which stocks to throw away
questions.why: The book shows the covers, the timing of the rush and any large party, which together decide how much sauce and garnish the station needs.

questions.q: Which of these belongs in a sauce station's mise en place before service?
questions.answer: Warm clarified butter and a strained reduction
distractors: Raw bones roasting for tomorrow's stock
Hollandaise made at noon and kept on the flame
Unpicked herbs to sort at the first order
questions.why: The slow parts of a warm emulsion are made before service, so a hollandaise or béarnaise can be finished in minutes when the ticket comes.

questions.q: Which details belong on the label of a container going into the fridge?
questions.answer: Its name, the date, initials and a use-by date
distractors: The supplier's phone number and the price
The station it came from and nothing else
The name of the dish it will be served on
questions.why: The name, the date, the initials and the use-by date tell any cook what it is, who made it and whether it can still be used.

questions.q: Under the FDA Food Code, how long may most chilled, ready-to-eat prepared food be kept?
questions.answer: Seven days, counting the day it was made
distractors: Fourteen days from the day after it was made
Thirty days if the lid is sealed
questions.why: Held at 5°C (41°F) or colder, most perishable ready-to-eat food made in the kitchen is used or thrown away within seven days, day one being the day it was made.

questions.q: At Brennan's, where does a server learn which Gulf fish is running today?
distractors: From the plate as it leaves the pass
questions.why: The fish changes with what is fresh, so the house teaches today's catch at lineup, the server's own mise en place before the doors open.

entries.title: Knife cuts
entries.summary: The classical knife cuts give every vegetable a named shape and size, from the tiny brunoise to the large dice, so that pieces cook evenly, look clean on the plate and yield the same every time.
entries.guest: Classically, vegetables are cut to one even size, so every piece cooks in the same time and softens together in the sauce.

paras: A knife cut is a shape and a size with a name. French kitchens fixed the names so that a chef can call for brunoise or julienne and every cook on the line cuts the same piece. Even cuts matter for three reasons. Pieces of one size cook in one time, so nothing stays raw while its neighbour turns to mush. They look clean, which shows in a clear sauce where every piece is visible. And they yield predictably: a cook who cuts evenly knows how many portions a case of onions will make.

Hold the knife in a pinch grip: the thumb and the side of the forefinger pinch the blade just ahead of the bolster, the thick join of blade and handle, and the other fingers wrap the handle. The guiding hand makes the claw: fingertips curled under, thumb tucked behind, so the flat of the blade rides against the knuckles. The knuckle is the guide. Move it back a little and the next slice is that much thicker, while the fingertips stay out of the way.

Square the vegetable first. Trim a carrot or potato into a neat block so it lies flat, cut planks of the thickness wanted, stack them, cut sticks, then cut the sticks across into dice. The trimmings go to stock or purée, not the bin.

The classical sizes run as a ladder. Julienne is a stick about 3 mm (1/8 inch) square and 5 to 6 cm (about 2 inches) long; cut across, it gives brunoise (broon-WAHZ), cubes about 3 mm (1/8 inch). Bâtonnet is a stick about 6 mm (1/4 inch) square and 6 cm (about 2 1/4 inches) long; cut across, it gives small dice. Medium dice is about 12 mm (1/2 inch) and large dice about 20 mm (3/4 inch). Schools vary a little; follow the recipe and the chef.

Some cuts are named for the job. To ciseler (seez-LAY) a shallot, halve it through the root, make thin lengthwise cuts towards the root without cutting through it, make one or two flat cuts parallel to the board, then slice down across the cuts into fine dice: the root holds it together, so it is cut, not crushed. Émincer (ay-man-SAY) is to slice thinly. Chiffonade (shif-uh-NAHD) is for leaves, stacked, rolled tight and sliced across into ribbons. Concassée (kohn-ka-SAY) is tomato peeled, seeded and chopped: score it, drop it into boiling water for 10 to 15 seconds, refresh it in iced water, slip off the skin, scoop out the seeds and chop.

Two cuts belong to the classical garnishes. Paysanne (pay-ee-ZAHN), country style, is thin tiles about 12 mm (1/2 inch) across and 3 mm (1/8 inch) thick, following the vegetable's shape, for soups. To tourner (toor-NAY) is to turn a potato or carrot into a small barrel with seven even faces, about 5 cm (2 inches) long: a slow test of a steady hand.

The holy trinity, onion, celery and green pepper, is classically cut to an even small dice so the three soften together in the fat; uneven pieces leave the small ones scorching while the large ones stay crunchy. At Brennan's it starts the Seafood Gumbo and the Turtle Soup, taught under The holy trinity; how fine the kitchen cuts it is a question for the chef.

A sharp knife is the careful knife. A dull edge needs force, slips off an onion's skin and goes where the cook never meant it to. Hone on a steel before each session and through the day: honing straightens the fine edge that bends with use. Sharpening on a whetstone grinds new metal into a fresh edge and is needed far less often. Keep the board on its damp cloth, never leave a knife in a sink of water, and carry it point down at your side, calling out as you pass.

On the floor, the cuts give a server words for what the guest sees: the tiny even cubes in a sauce are brunoise, the fine ribbons of herb are chiffonade. A guest who asks why the vegetables are all so soft and even hears the plain truth: they were cut to one size, so they cooked in one time. The names as they appear on a menu or ticket are taught under Cuts by name.

ratios.label: Julienne
ratios.value: About 3 mm (1/8 inch) square, 5 to 6 cm (about 2 inches) long

ratios.label: Bâtonnet
ratios.value: About 6 mm (1/4 inch) square, about 6 cm (2 1/4 inches) long

ratios.label: Paysanne
ratios.value: Tiles about 12 mm (1/2 inch) across, 3 mm (1/8 inch) thick

faults.cause: The vegetable was not squared, or the planks and sticks were cut by guesswork.
faults.fix: Square the vegetable into a block, cut even planks, then even sticks, and only then cut across into dice.

faults.fault: Crushed, wet shallots or bruised herbs
faults.cause: A dull knife, or a rocking, chopping stroke that crushes rather than slices.
faults.fix: Hone the edge and slice with clean strokes; cut a chiffonade close to service so the leaves stay green.

faults.fault: Pieces that scorch while others stay hard
faults.cause: Mixed sizes in one pan, such as a trinity cut unevenly.
faults.fix: Cut everything that cooks together to one size, so it softens in one time.

faults.cause: No damp cloth or non-slip mat beneath it.
faults.fix: Set a damp cloth or mat under the board before the first cut.

brennans.how: The Seafood Gumbo starts with the holy trinity, onion, celery and green pepper softened together, which is why the cut matters: even pieces soften in one time. How fine the kitchen cuts it is a question for the chef.
The Turtle Soup is built on the trinity too, softened together at the start of the soup; how fine the kitchen cuts it is a question for the chef.

cards.front: Why do cooks cut vegetables to one even size?
cards.back: Even pieces cook in the same time, look clean in a clear sauce and give a predictable yield from every case.

cards.front: What is the pinch grip on a chef's knife?
cards.back: Thumb and the side of the forefinger pinch the blade just ahead of the bolster, the other fingers wrapped round the handle, for control.

cards.front: How does the guiding hand hold the food?
cards.back: In a claw: fingertips curled under and thumb tucked behind, so the blade rides against the knuckles and the fingertips stay clear.

cards.front: How big is a brunoise, and how is it cut?
cards.back: Cubes about 3 mm (1/8 inch), cut by slicing julienne sticks across at the same width.

cards.front: What are the measurements of a julienne?
cards.back: A stick about 3 mm (1/8 inch) square and 5 to 6 cm (about 2 inches) long.

cards.front: Give the sizes of small, medium and large dice.
cards.back: Small about 6 mm (1/4 inch), medium about 12 mm (1/2 inch) and large about 20 mm (3/4 inch).

cards.front: What are tourner and paysanne?
cards.back: Two cuts of the classical garnishes: tourner trims a vegetable into a seven-faced barrel about 5 cm (2 inches) long; paysanne is thin tiles about 3 mm (1/8 inch) thick.

cards.front: How do you ciseler a shallot?
cards.back: Halve it through the root, cut thin lengthwise slices towards the root without cutting through, make one or two flat cuts parallel to the board, then slice across into fine dice.

cards.front: How is a chiffonade of leaves cut?
cards.back: Stack the leaves, roll them tightly and slice across the roll into fine ribbons with a sharp knife.

cards.front: What is tomato concassée?
cards.back: Tomato peeled, seeded and chopped: scored, dropped into boiling water for 10 to 15 seconds, refreshed in iced water, skinned, seeded and diced.

cards.front: Why is the holy trinity cut to an even small dice?
cards.back: So onion, celery and green pepper soften together in the fat, with no small pieces scorching and no large ones left crunchy.

cards.front: What is the difference between honing and sharpening?
cards.back: Honing on a steel straightens the edge that bends with use; sharpening on a stone grinds away metal to make a fresh edge.

questions.q: What is the main reason a kitchen cuts vegetables to one even size?
questions.answer: So every piece cooks in the same time
distractors: So the knife stays sharp for longer
So the dish needs less salt
So the vegetables can be cut faster
questions.why: Pieces of one size cook in one time, so none is raw while its neighbour turns to mush; a clean look and a steady yield follow.

questions.q: In the claw grip, what guides the side of the blade?
questions.answer: The knuckles of the guiding hand
questions.why: The fingertips curl under and the blade rides against the knuckles, which set each slice's thickness and keep the fingertips out of reach.

questions.q: Roughly how big is a classical brunoise cube?
questions.why: Brunoise is julienne cut across at the same width, so its cubes are about 3 mm (1/8 inch) on every side.

questions.q: Which size is a classical medium dice?
questions.why: The dice run small at about 6 mm, medium at about 12 mm and large at about 20 mm; 3 mm is brunoise.

questions.q: Which cut is a stick about 3 mm square and 5 to 6 cm long?
questions.why: Julienne is the fine stick; bâtonnet is twice as thick, paysanne is a thin tile and chiffonade is ribbons of leaf.

questions.q: Why is a shallot ciselé with its root left on?
questions.answer: The root holds the layers together
distractors: The root adds sweetness to the sauce
The root keeps the shallot from browning
The root is the part that is served
questions.why: Left whole at the root, the shallot stays in one piece through the cuts, so the last slices fall away as fine, even dice.

questions.q: What does concassée mean for a tomato?
distractors: Sliced thinly with the skin on
Cooked down to a thick paste
questions.why: The tomato is scored, blanched for a few seconds, refreshed in iced water, skinned and seeded, and only the flesh is chopped.

questions.q: Why is the holy trinity cut to an even small dice?
questions.answer: So the three vegetables soften together
distractors: So the celery stays crunchy in the gumbo
So the pepper can be picked out later
So it can be served raw as a garnish
questions.why: Onion, celery and green pepper cut to one size soften in one time, with no pieces scorching and none left hard.

questions.q: What does honing a knife on a steel do?
questions.answer: Straightens the edge that bends with use
distractors: Grinds away metal to make a new edge
Coats the blade so food does not stick
Removes rust from the handle rivets
questions.why: Honing realigns the fine edge through the day; sharpening on a stone, which removes metal, is needed far less often.

questions.q: Which classical garnish cut trims a potato or carrot into a small barrel with seven even faces?
questions.why: To tourner is to turn a vegetable into a seven-faced barrel about 5 cm (2 inches) long; paysanne is thin tiles, brunoise tiny cubes and bâtonnet a stick.

entries.title: Heat and the pan
entries.say: As it reads: heat and the pan.
entries.summary: How heat travels into food, why browning needs a hot, dry surface, how the stove's heat ladder and each kind of pan behave, and how a cook reads heat with the ear, the eye, the nose and the probe.
entries.guest: The golden crust comes from a hot, dry pan: the surface browns quickly while the inside stays moist and tender.

paras: Every cooking method is a way of moving heat into food, and heat travels three ways. Conduction passes it by touch, from flame to pan to food, which is why a steak browns where it meets the metal. Convection carries it through a moving liquid or gas: oil in a fryer, water in a pot, the hot air of an oven. Radiation crosses open space, from the glowing salamander, the overhead grill above the line, or from coals beneath a grill.

Browning gives much of the flavour, through two reactions. The Maillard reaction joins proteins and sugars into hundreds of new flavours and a brown colour; it is slow at lower heat and quick from about 140°C (284°F), the crust on seared meat, toast and roasted coffee. Caramelisation is sugar alone breaking down at higher heat, from roughly 160 to 170°C (320 to 338°F) for table sugar, giving the sweet, bitter notes of caramel.

Water sets the limit. At sea level, as in New Orleans, water boils at 100°C (212°F), and food in water or steam cannot rise above that at its surface, far below browning heat. So a poached or boiled food never browns, and a wet steak, or a pan so crowded that the juices cannot evaporate, steams grey instead of searing. Dry the surface, heat the pan first and leave space between the pieces.

The heat ladder, in outline: low heat melts butter, softens vegetables without colour and keeps a sauce warm; medium heat cooks eggs and turns onions golden; high heat sears, browns and brings water to a fast boil. Tell a simmer from a boil by the bubbles. At a simmer, small bubbles rise lazily and break at the surface; at a boil, large bubbles roll without stopping and keep rolling when stirred.

Read heat with every sense. Food laid in a hot pan sizzles at once; silence means the pan was cold. Oil shimmers when it is hot enough to sauté and smokes when it starts to burn. Browning smells toasty; burning smells sharp and acrid. Then use the probe, an instant-read thermometer, in the thickest part and away from bone, checked in iced water, where it reads 0°C (32°F).

Heat does not stop when food leaves the pan. The outside is hotter than the centre and that stored heat keeps moving inwards, so a thick roast taken out at 52°C (126°F) in the centre may reach about 57°C (135°F) as it rests. Thick food carries over more than thin, so cooks take it off a little early and let it rest.

Pans each have a job. Heavy pans hold heat and spread it evenly, so they recover quickly when cold food goes in; thin pans heat and cool fast and form hot spots. Cast iron is slow to heat but holds it like a stone, for searing and blackening. Stainless steel bonded round an aluminium or copper core is the all-rounder: it does not react with acid, and it keeps the fond, the browned film a pan sauce is built on.

Copper answers the flame fastest and most evenly, lined with tin or steel because bare copper reacts with food. Non-stick is for eggs and delicate fish at moderate heat. Bare aluminium conducts well and costs little, but it reacts with acid: tomato, wine or lemon cooked in it can taste metallic, and a white sauce whisked in it can turn grey.

Blackening is cast iron at its limit: in the classic method, food is dipped in melted butter, coated in spice and laid in a dry cast-iron skillet heated past smoking, where butter and spice char to a dark crust in about two minutes a side for a fish fillet while the inside stays moist. It throws heavy smoke, so the hood runs on full. The Blackened Tofu uses the method, and Blackening has its own entry. Frying is convection in oil: at about 175 to 190°C (347 to 374°F) the coating browns fast while the inside steams, as on the Popcorn Shrimp, taught under Frying. Questions about butter, coatings, shared fryers or the oil go to the kitchen.
At the table, heat becomes the words for texture: a golden crust from a hot pan, tenderness from a slow simmer. Use them only for what tonight's dish truly is, as learned at lineup.

faults.fault: Grey, steamed meat with no crust
faults.cause: A wet surface, a pan not yet hot, or a pan so crowded that the juices pool.
faults.fix: Pat the food dry, heat the pan before the fat and food go in, and cook in batches with space between pieces.

faults.cause: Heat too high for the thickness of the piece.
faults.fix: Brown it hot, then lower the heat or finish it in the oven until the centre is cooked.

faults.cause: The pan was not hot enough, or the food was moved before its crust formed.
faults.fix: Heat the pan first and leave the food alone; once the crust has set it releases by itself.

faults.fault: A metallic taste or a grey white sauce
faults.cause: Acid cooked, or a white sauce whisked, in bare aluminium.
faults.fix: Use stainless steel, enamelled cast iron or lined copper for anything acidic or white.

faults.cause: Carryover heat was not allowed for.
faults.fix: Take thick food off the heat a little before its target and let it rest.

brennans.how: The Blackened Tofu uses Paul Prudhomme's blackening method: spiced and seared in a dry cast-iron pan heated past smoking. The classic method dips the food in melted butter first, which is why the kitchen is asked before the dish is called vegan.
The Popcorn Shrimp are fried in hot oil, convection at work: the coating browns and crisps while the shrimp steam inside. Questions about the coating, shared fryers or the oil go to the kitchen.

cards.front: What are the three ways heat reaches food?
cards.back: Conduction by touch through the pan, convection in moving oil, water or air, and radiation across space from a salamander or coals.

cards.front: What is a salamander, and how does it heat food?
cards.back: The overhead grill above the line; it cooks by radiation, glowing heat sent across open space onto the top of the food.

cards.front: What is the Maillard reaction?
cards.back: The browning of proteins and sugars together into new flavours and a brown colour, quick from about 140°C (284°F): the crust on seared meat and toast.

cards.front: How does caramelisation differ from the Maillard reaction?
cards.back: Caramelisation is sugar alone breaking down at higher heat, table sugar from roughly 160 to 170°C (320 to 338°F); Maillard needs protein as well as sugar.

cards.front: Why does a poached or boiled food never brown?
cards.back: Water cannot get hotter than 100°C (212°F) at sea level, well below the heat browning needs.

cards.front: Why does a crowded pan steam instead of searing?
cards.back: The pieces give off more juice than can evaporate, so they sit in liquid held near 100°C (212°F) and turn grey rather than brown.

cards.front: How do you tell a simmer from a boil?
cards.back: At a simmer, small bubbles rise lazily and break at the surface; at a boil, large bubbles roll constantly and keep rolling when stirred.

cards.front: What does a heavy pan do that a thin one cannot?
cards.back: It holds heat and spreads it evenly, so it recovers fast when cold food goes in; a thin pan reacts quickly and forms hot spots.

cards.front: Why not cook tomato or wine in bare aluminium?
cards.back: Bare aluminium reacts with acid, giving a metallic taste, and can turn a white sauce grey; use stainless steel or enamel instead.

cards.front: What is carryover heat in cooking?
cards.back: Heat stored in the outside of food keeps moving inwards after it leaves the heat, so food comes off a little early and rests.

cards.front: What do the sizzle, the shimmer and the smoke tell a cook about a pan?
cards.back: A sizzle as food goes in means the pan is hot, silence means cold; oil shimmers when ready to sauté and smokes as it starts to burn. Only blackening goes past smoking on purpose, with butter-dipped food in dry cast iron.

cards.front: How do you check an instant-read thermometer?
cards.back: Stand the probe in iced water: it should read 0°C (32°F). Then read food in its thickest part, away from bone.

questions.q: Which way of moving heat cooks food in a deep fryer?
questions.why: Hot oil moves around the food and carries heat into it, which is convection, the same way water heats food in a pot.

questions.q: A salamander browns the top of a dish mainly by which kind of heat?
questions.why: The salamander's glowing element sends heat across open space onto the food, which is radiation, as from coals beneath a grill.

questions.q: The Maillard reaction browns food by joining which two things?
questions.why: Maillard browning needs protein and sugar together; sugar alone breaking down at higher heat is caramelisation.

questions.q: Roughly where does table sugar begin to caramelise?
questions.why: Table sugar starts to break down into caramel at roughly 160 to 170°C (320 to 338°F), hotter than Maillard browning gets going.

questions.q: Why does a crowded pan turn a steak grey instead of brown?
questions.answer: Its juices cannot boil off, so it steams
distractors: The pan gets too hot and burns it
The salt draws out all the colour
The fat soaks into the meat
questions.why: Packed pieces release more liquid than can boil away, and food in liquid stays near 100°C (212°F), too cool to brown.

questions.q: Why can a boiled potato never brown in the pot?
distractors: Potatoes hold no sugar at all
Salt in the water stops browning
questions.why: At sea level water cannot rise above 100°C (212°F), well below browning heat, so anything cooked in it stays pale.

questions.q: Which pan is the poor choice for a long-simmered tomato sauce?
questions.why: Bare aluminium reacts with the acid in tomato, giving a metallic taste; stainless steel, enamel and lined copper do not.

questions.q: Why does a cook take a thick roast off the heat before it reaches the target temperature?
questions.answer: Carryover heat finishes it as it rests
distractors: The thermometer always reads too low
The oven is hottest in its final minutes
So the juices settle before it is carved
questions.why: Heat stored in the outside keeps moving to the centre after the roast comes out, so it climbs a little further as it rests.

questions.q: An instant-read thermometer stands in iced water. What should it read?
questions.why: Iced water sits at the freezing point, 0°C (32°F), so a probe that reads anything else needs adjusting before it is trusted.

questions.q: In the classic blackening method, what is the food dipped in before its spice coating?
questions.why: Prudhomme dipped the fillet in melted butter before the spice, and that butter is why the kitchen is asked before the Blackened Tofu is called vegan.

entries.title: White stock
entries.say: As it reads: white stock, or fond blanc, fohn BLAHN.
entries.summary: Fond blanc, white stock, is chicken or veal bones simmered gently from cold water with a pale mirepoix and herbs, never roasted, for a clear, light, gelatinous liquid that becomes velouté, suprême, allemande and the white soups.
entries.guest: A velouté starts from white stock: chicken or veal bones simmered slowly for hours, which gives the sauce its body and a clean, savoury depth.

paras: White stock, fond blanc (fohn BLAHN) in French, is the pale stock of the classical kitchen: chicken or veal bones simmered slowly in water with vegetables and herbs, then strained. Nothing is browned. The bones are blanched or rinsed, never roasted, and the vegetables go in raw, so the stock stays pale, clear and light, tasting of the bones rather than of a roasting pan. Fond means base, and that is its job: it is a building block, not a soup.

A good white stock is judged cold. Its body is gelatine, drawn from the collagen in knuckles, joints, wings and feet by hours of gentle heat, and a stock with enough of it sets to a soft wobble in the fridge. That gelatine gives a sauce its silky feel and lets it reduce to a gloss.

Cut the bones to fit the pot: veal knuckles, or chicken carcasses, necks, wings and feet. For the clearest stock, blanch them: cover with cold water, bring to the boil, drain and rinse away the grey scum. Chicken bones are often only rinsed well, which keeps more flavour.

Cover the bones with cold water by about 5 cm (2 inches). Starting cold matters: as the water warms slowly, the proteins that would cloud the stock gather into scum and rise, where they can be skimmed. Bring it slowly to a bare simmer, around 85 to 90°C (185 to 194°F), the surface just trembling, and skim as the scum and fat gather. Never let it boil: boiling churns fat and protein back into the liquid and leaves it cloudy and greasy.

Once the first heavy scum is off, add the white mirepoix, onion, celery and leek in large pieces, with a bouquet garni of thyme, bay and parsley stalks tied in a leek leaf, and a few peppercorns. Some kitchens add a little carrot; the white mirepoix leaves it out for the palest stock. Simmer chicken about 3 to 5 hours and veal 6 to 8, topping up with cold water if the bones show. Add no salt: the stock will be reduced, and salt concentrates with it.
Ladle the stock out, rather than tipping the pot, through a chinois, the fine conical sieve, lined with muslin for the clearest result. Cool it fast, then lift off the fat once it has set on top.

A working proportion is about 4 kg (about 9 lb) of bones to 6 litres (about 6 quarts) of cold water and 500 g (1 lb) of white mirepoix, roughly one part vegetables to eight of bones by weight, for about 4 litres (about 1 gallon) of finished stock. More bones give a richer stock; more water gives a thin one that never sets.

White stock is the liquid of the velouté family. Thickened with a blond roux it becomes velouté; chicken velouté reduced with cream becomes suprême; veal velouté bound with egg yolks and sharpened with lemon becomes allemande (Escoffier's also took mushroom liquor and no cream; many kitchens today use a yolk and cream liaison). It makes the cream soups, poaches a chicken and cooks a blanquette, the veal stew in a white sauce. Escoffier began his Guide Culinaire (1903) with the stocks, the fonds de cuisine, before a single sauce.

Most faults come from heat and haste. A cloudy stock was boiled, stirred or left unskimmed; straining through damp muslin helps, though only a raft, taught under Clarifying, will make it fully clear again. A thin stock that will not set had too much water, too few joints or too little time: reduce it gently. A bitter edge comes from vegetables and peppercorns left in too long, or from scorching on the bottom of the pot.

Guests rarely see stock, but they meet it in every velouté, cream soup and white braise. A soup or sauce built on chicken or veal stock carries meat even when nothing on the plate looks like meat, so a guest who avoids meat, or eats vegetarian, gets the answer from the kitchen, never a guess from the server.

ratios.label: Bones to cold water
ratios.value: About 4 kg (about 9 lb) to 6 litres (about 6 quarts)

ratios.label: White mirepoix to bones
ratios.value: About one part to eight by weight, 500 g (1 lb) for 4 kg of bones

ratios.label: Simmering time
ratios.value: Chicken about 3 to 5 hours, veal about 6 to 8 hours

ratios.label: Yield
ratios.value: About 4 litres (about 1 gallon) of finished stock

temps.label: A bare simmer, the surface just trembling
The top of a bare simmer
A boil, which a stock must never reach

faults.cause: It was boiled, stirred, started in hot water or left unskimmed.
faults.fix: Strain it through damp muslin; next time start cold, hold a bare simmer and skim often.

faults.cause: Boiling emulsified the fat into the liquid, or it was never degreased.
faults.fix: Chill it and lift off the set fat; keep the next batch below the boil.

faults.fault: Thin stock that will not set
faults.cause: Too much water, too few joints and wings, or too short a simmer.
faults.fix: Reduce it gently; next time add knuckles, wings or feet and give it the full time.

faults.cause: The bones were not blanched or rinsed, or the vegetables cooked to mush.
faults.fix: Blanch or rinse the bones, and add the mirepoix only once the first scum is off.

faults.cause: Vegetables and peppercorns left in too long, or bones scorched on the bottom.
faults.fix: Keep the heat low, keep the bones covered and strain the stock as soon as it is done.

cards.front: What makes a white stock white?
cards.back: Nothing is browned: the bones are blanched or rinsed, never roasted, and the vegetables go in raw, so the stock stays pale and clean.

cards.front: Which bones make a white stock, and why those?
cards.back: Chicken carcasses, necks, wings and feet, or veal knuckles, chosen for their joints because their collagen becomes gelatine.

cards.front: Why blanch the bones for a white stock?
cards.back: Bringing them to the boil from cold water, then draining and rinsing, removes the blood and scum that would cloud and grey the stock.

cards.front: Why does a stock start in cold water?
cards.back: As the water warms slowly, the proteins that would cloud it gather into scum and rise, where they can be skimmed off.

cards.front: Why must a white stock never boil?
cards.back: Boiling churns fat and protein back into the liquid, leaving it cloudy and greasy; a bare simmer, around 85 to 90°C (185 to 194°F), keeps it clear.

cards.front: What goes into a white mirepoix and its bouquet garni?
cards.back: Onion, celery and leek, with no carrot for the palest stock; thyme, bay and parsley stalks tied in a leek leaf, and a few peppercorns.

cards.front: How long do chicken and veal white stocks simmer?
cards.back: Chicken about 3 to 5 hours and veal about 6 to 8, topped up with cold water if the bones show.

cards.front: Why is a stock never salted?
cards.back: It will be reduced for sauces and glaces, and salt concentrates as the water goes, so a salted stock ends too salty.

cards.front: How do you know a white stock has enough gelatine?
cards.back: It sets to a soft wobble when cold; the gelatine from the joints gives sauces a silky body and a gloss when reduced.

cards.front: What is a working ratio for white stock?
cards.back: About 4 kg (about 9 lb) of bones to 6 litres (about 6 quarts) of water and 500 g (1 lb) of white mirepoix, for about 4 litres.

cards.front: Name three sauces built on white stock.
cards.back: Velouté, with a blond roux; suprême, chicken velouté reduced with cream; and allemande, veal velouté bound with egg yolks and lemon, often with cream today.

cards.front: A guest who avoids meat asks about a cream soup. What does the server do?
cards.back: Asks the kitchen. A soup or sauce made with chicken or veal stock carries meat even when nothing on the plate looks like meat.

questions.q: What keeps a white stock pale and clean?
questions.answer: Bones blanched or rinsed, never roasted
distractors: Chicken bones only, never any veal
A splash of milk added as the stock simmers
questions.why: Nothing in a white stock is browned, so it tastes of the bones and stays pale; roasting and tomato belong to brown stock.

questions.q: Why do the bones go into cold water rather than boiling water?
questions.answer: So the scum gathers and rises
distractors: So the bones brown as the water heats
So the stock boils over less often
So the vegetables cook before the bones
questions.why: Warming slowly from cold lets the clouding proteins gather into a scum that floats, so the cook can lift it off.

questions.q: What happens when a white stock is left at a rolling boil?
distractors: It sets more firmly when cold
questions.why: Boiling churns fat and protein back into the liquid; a bare simmer, the surface just trembling, keeps the stock clear.

questions.q: Which vegetable does a white mirepoix leave out for the palest stock?
questions.why: The white mirepoix is onion, celery and leek; carrot would tint the stock, though some kitchens add a little.

questions.q: Roughly how long does a veal white stock simmer?
questions.why: Veal bones need 6 to 8 hours of gentle heat to give up their gelatine; chicken takes about 3 to 5.

questions.q: Why is no salt added to a white stock?
distractors: Salt clouds the stock as it simmers
Salt stops the gelatine from setting
questions.why: Stock is reduced for sauces and glaces; the water goes but the salt stays, so any salt added early ends far too strong.

questions.q: How do you know a white stock has plenty of gelatine?
questions.answer: It sets to a soft wobble when cold
distractors: It stays runny in the fridge
It turns cloudy as it cools
questions.why: Gelatine from the collagen in joints sets the cold stock to a jelly and gives the sauces made from it their body.

questions.q: Which sauce is a white stock thickened with a blond roux?
questions.why: Velouté is white stock with a blond roux; béchamel is milk with a white roux, and espagnole is built on brown stock.

questions.q: A guest who avoids meat asks whether a cream soup is made with stock. What does the server do?
distractors: Say cream soups never use stock
Guess from how the soup looks
Tell the guest it tastes of vegetables
questions.why: A soup built on chicken or veal stock carries meat even when none shows, so only the kitchen can answer.
